title: Clancy Wilmott - Adventures at the Limits of Spatial Data from the Pixel to the Pacific
transcriptText:
HENRY BRADY: Welcome, everybody.
Great to see you here.
This is our second lecture
in a series of lectures
on human technology futures.
I'm Henry Brady, I'm the
former dean and a professor
in the Goldman School of Public
Policy and the political science
department.
I'm also one of the cofounders
of BIDS, the Berkeley
Institute of Data Science.
So I have a long-running
interest, decades at this point,
in data science
and its importance,
but also in the impact
of data science,
artificial intelligence,
and other stuff like that
on human futures.
And so that's why I'm very
excited about the human futures
enterprise.
Today, we're lucky to
have Clancy Wilmott,
who's an assistant professor
in critical cartography--
these are big words--
geovisualization and design
at the Berkeley Center
for New Media and the
Department of Geography.
She comes to UC Berkeley from
the Department of Geography
at the University of
Manchester, where she received
her PhD in human geography
with a multisite study
on the interaction between
mobile phone use and maps,
cartographic discourse,
discussions of maps,
and postcolonial
landscapes in places where
there had been colonial powers.
Fascinating set of issues.
It turns out, cell phones are
really important, for example,
in places like Africa and
have really revolutionized
the way things are
done in that country.
She holds undergraduate
degrees in communications
and international
studies as well as
postgraduate degree
in cultural studies
from the University
of Technology, Sydney.
She's the author
of Mobile Mapping--
Space, Cartography and the
Digital, published in 2020.
The book argues for a
theory of mobile mapping,
a situated and spatial
approach towards researching
how everyday
digital mobile media
practices are bound up in global
systems of knowledge and power.
She also has published
papers in the Annals
of the Association of
American Geographers, Big Data
and Society, The
Leonardo Electronic
Almanac, and The Journal of
Television and New Media,
among others.
Her current work is on--
it's in small print--
cartophobia--
CLANCY WILMOTT: Cartotopia.
HENRY BRADY: --cartopeia,
another one of those hard
words--
and an atlas of artificial
intelligence maps.
So that sounds fascinating.
And today, she's going to talk
about Computation as Critique--
Adventures at the Limits of
Spatial Data from the Pixel
to the Pacific.
Clancy.
CLANCY WILMOTT: Thank you.
Thank you very much.
So computation as critique--
I'm going to just speed
through this presentation
today because I want
to make sure there's
plenty of time for conversation,
plenty of times for questions.
And when Catherine asked
me to present today,
I thought I'd actually
maybe approach
the elephant in the
room head-on, which
is this question of what
do we mean by critique,
this thing that apparently
divides the humanities and STEM
disciplines, this question.
And I spend a lot of time
thinking about this question
because one of the benefits
of being a geographer
is I'm pretty much
squarely in the middle.
As geographers, I
will sit in a room
with geochemists,
geophysicists, geomorphologists.
Many of my colleagues
were trained in ecology,
in data science,
sometimes in forms
of experimental archeology.
So it's very
multidisciplinary discipline.
And we've had a lot
of these conversations
over the last 20 or so years
about this question of critique.
For me, as someone
who makes maps,
it basically poses this
fundamental dilemma
that we face which, on one hand,
our maps don't work particularly
well.
They inherit
long-standing problems
in terms of the way in which
maps and map-making has been
used to conquer
territories, to displace
people, the limitations of
representation and abstraction.
I remember reading a really
interesting conversation
that Newton was having about the
relationship between physicists
and mathematicians about
this question of abstraction.
So we know that there
are limitations there.
We also know that the
maps that we have,
the systems of spatial
data that we have,
are not particularly
good at representing
non-Western conceptions
of space, time, and place.
But-- and this is the
question of critique--
on the other hand,
what we also know
is that despite all
of these limitations,
despite these critiques and
the way in which mapping is
imbricated in systems
of knowledge power,
we also know that mapping
GIS and cartography
are really valuable.
They're absolutely
central to the production
of scientific knowledge,
scientific knowledge which
actually prevents entire
communities from falling harm
to pollutants or other kinds
of environmental injustices.
We know that it's important
to environmental monitoring,
to the point where you're giving
Indigenous people GPS devices
to actually monitor
changes in the Amazon.
We know that spatial
storytelling, crisis response,
humanitarian disaster response--
so one of the first things
that will happen when
there's a major earthquake
or disaster in places
like Haiti or Africa
is you'll have people trying
to struggle to find maps.
And the quality of your map
depends on the quality of aid
you can deliver.
We also know that
it's actually really
important to visual
and spatial computing.
How do we get these
cars, like the Waymos,
to drive around without
crashing into things?
As well as infrastructural
engineering,
it's very difficult
to build a city
or to make a road without using
a map or a plan or something
cartographic in that process.
So we have this dilemma.
And my favorite place to be as
a scholar is kind of squarely
in the middle.
I love this middle space,
and so most of my research
is coming at this set of
questions from both sides.
On one hand,
reading, theorizing,
undertaking historical
and archival analysis of,
what does this mean?
We got a grant for
my research group
to spend an entire year just
asking the one question,
what makes a map colonial?
And the problem that we found
is that every culture has maps.
Every culture makes maps.
Every culture has mathematics.
Every culture has systems
of counting and calculation.
And that, fundamentally, one of
the problems of Western mapping
is not the mathematics,
not the calculation, not
the inherent
algorithms, but actually
just a more fundamental
idea around progress
that things have
to keep growing,
that the map itself, as a
Cartesian basis, expands.
That's what it's designed to do.
But, of course, our
Earth is not expanding.
And so we've got this
fundamental problem.
But at the same time, I do
actually literally make maps.
I make a lot of maps.
I do a lot of computation.
I do a lot of coding.
I do everything from
experimental stuff
down to really
basic data science.
And I teach across all
of these domains as well.
And increasingly,
I'm finding that I'm
having to teach the Pythagorean
theorem to students as they
come in.
I'm like, what is that?
OK, let's do some
basic geometry.
The way that I situate
this set of questions
is in these two maps.
And so those of you
in computer science,
data science are probably
going yeah, but--
so I'm going to introduce you
to a profoundly geographical
problem.
Why do I sit in this place
when you guys are here
but we have vectors?
Yeah, but we've got
all these other things
that have happened since then.
The problem is geography
hasn't really moved on.
And certainly the way in which
we represent space and spatial
process from a
geographical perspective
is still resolutely based
in historical systems
that have been around
for hundreds of years.
And so this is a map of a
city, of a river, Dyarubbin,
which is in the west of Sydney.
On one hand, you have
a map by Dawes in 1793.
So this was the first survey
party that went out West.
And this is the
map that they made
as part of an account of the
settlement at Port Jackson
and sent back to London
for people to read.
This is the first
map that they made.
And it was pretty
legendary because this
was the point at
which they realized
it's actually two rivers.
It's the Hawkesbury at the top,
and then Nepean at the bottom.
They thought they were separate.
They managed to join them.
Took them five years to
actually do that whole area.
And actually, a
sort of weird aside
is that they had a
bunch of cows that
came on the first fleet that
escaped after six months,
and they thought they'd all
been eaten by local Indigenous
people.
But when they were doing
this, they actually
found that they were starving.
The settlers were starving.
The cows, however, had gone all
the way West to the Nepean River
and were completely thriving.
They were dozens of them.
And they called them the
free cow pastures of the--
that was basically
what they call them.
So you've got this
map on one hand,
and then, in 2024, you
have this other map,
which admittedly, there's a few
more graphical user interface
changes.
You've got some data
layers that you can put on.
You've maybe got some labeling.
You can zoom in and out.
It's what's called a slippy map.
But fundamentally, the way
in which this information
is being communicated is not
that fundamentally different
to this map.
The river is still a line.
The mountains are
still kind of absent.
It's unclear where
the settlement is.
And when you've got
two maps of rivers,
what is the point of mapping a
river if not to actually explain
not just where it is
but what it is like?
And this is where the
river as a thin line
becomes a major problem.
So Tench, who was the
surveyor with Dawes,
knew that this river
was incredible.
Dyarubbin is known
for huge floods.
So basically, what happens is
if I go back to this slide,
the water comes all the
way through the Nepean,
and at the very top, you
can see some red dots
near the mountains.
Basically, all the water
comes and then hits
this funnel and
then back washes,
and the entire
plain gets flooded.
And they've known this.
When they drew the
river as a line,
they knew that this was a fact.
Tench writes, "We proceeded
from there up to Richmond Hill
by the river side, mounted
it, slept at the foot,
and on the following day
penetrated some miles westward
or inland of it, until we
were stopped by a mountainous
country, which our
scarcity of provisions,
joined to the terror of
the river at our back,
whose sudden rising--" and this
is what I want to emphasize--
"whose sudden rising is
almost beyond computation."
So they knew that this
river would rise fast,
and yet they still
depicted it as a line.
Similarly, this
is my own writing,
but in 2022, we're
still experiencing
the same problems of floods.
The once-in-100-year flood
that was calculated to happen
actually happened twice,
thousands of displaced.
People die fairly
regularly with this river.
And the river that the map they
made after this major event--
so since 1790, there have
been more than 130 floods
recorded along Dyarubbin, which
have reached 10 meters or more.
So that's, what, 20 feet?
In 2022, that predicted
once-in-100-year flood occurred
twice, with thousands
evacuated each time.
So we have this major issue.
And yet, despite this,
the map they still made
was that map that you saw
on your right-hand side,
a line which has a
kind of area, what they
call probable maximum flood.
And on one hand, you
could argue this is just
a technical or graphic problem.
My argument is, actually, this
is a much more fundamental
problem to the way in which we
understand process and visualize
process.
We are stuck with a system
of coordinate geometry
that Descartes created for
a very specific purpose.
The fundamental
of GIS and mapping
is what we call points,
lines, and polygons.
We aren't even into 3D yet.
We can't even get to volume.
And let's not talk about
time because that's hard.
And so we have this
fundamental problem.
And despite all of these
advances in computation
in mathematics, the invention
or the creation of vectors
and vector calculus,
of algebraic geometry,
of different forms
of representation,
we're still in this very
flat coordinate geometry.
And when we shifted
from paper to digital,
we basically kept it the
same and added a GUI.
This is the fundamental
problem that I'm
trying to ask this question
because it has consequences,
this inability for us to think
and engage mathematically,
to engage computationally
with the map
beyond this historic structure.
And so part of that
is questioning,
well, what other structures
could we imagine or think of?
And so the question
I ask is, do we
have to settle for the
abstractions, geometries,
and taxonomies that
we've inherited
if they're not fit for purpose?
And so this makes me a
minor renegade in geography.
People are like, oh, I
don't know about this.
I'm like, well,
there's nothing natural
that says that the map
has to be like this.
We can create cubes.
We can create diagrams.
We can create network maps.
We can create any
number of things.
We could create robots,
if we wanted to,
that make complex maps.
We don't have to
accept those maps.
We don't have to accept
those hierarchies
of the way in which
data is classified,
those classifications.
We don't have to accept those
forms of geometry either.
But then the question is,
well, what do we do instead?
And so I do two things.
One of the things I do is I work
with different organizations
that have questions
about the map and to see
what happens if we just say
yes to every request they have.
And so I got approached
by Sogorea Te' Land Trust,
who wanted a map of Indigenous
land in the Bay area,
and I was like, OK, guys,
this sounds like fun.
And it ended up taking
three years for us
to make this map, three years
of constant collaboration
because it was quite
a computational feat.
But the questions
that they were asking
were also fundamentally
critical of the geometry
that they had
basically inherited.
The first question I
asked them was like,
well, we have a 0, 0 on the map.
And that 0, 0, if you
have a look it up,
there used to be a Google
review for a supermarket at 0,
0 that someone left there,
"best supermarket in the world,"
but it's a completely
abstracted, meaningless point.
It has computational meaning,
but no social meaning off
the West Coast of Africa.
And I asked, Sogorea
Te', do you like 0, 0?
They're like, but
how do we come by it?
I'm like, well,
it's the equator,
which is the widest part of the
Earth, which is not a sphere.
It is a geoid.
It moves.
It's kind of magnetic.
But also the longitudinal line,
that was decided in the 1880s
at the World
Meridian Conference.
And there were
three competitors--
Paris, London, and Washington.
London had the largest
navy, so London won out.
And the Greenwich Meridian
now runs through the Royal
Observatory at Greenwich, which
is on the Royal Naval grounds,
just outside London.
And I mean, it's useful
to all have things
together at a certain point in
time to have that universality,
particularly when you're doing
a lot of calculation by hand.
We don't really do
calculation by hand.
And in the 1990s, when we
switched from doing old-school
logarithmic projections on paper
and started using computers,
no one thought to ask,
oh, do we have to keep 0,
0 at the middle of
the British Empire?
I mean, isn't that kind of over?
Couldn't we compute
from anywhere?
Theoretically, yes.
Pragmatically, we didn't.
And so they're like, we want 0,
0 to be actually down in Oakland
in the Bay Area.
And I'm like, OK, cool.
So what's at the top of the map?
They're like, the top?
There's no top of the world.
I'm like, well, the
map's got to have a top.
Like, does it have
to have a top?
And I'm like, does the
map have to have a top?
Interesting question.
And I was like, well,
actually, we already
have practices in place
that allow us to make
maps that don't have a top.
Whenever we do a
projection of the poles,
it's what we call a
stereographic projection,
like this.
So this is the map that
we ended up making.
And so it's a series of
uneven concentric circles
that radiate outwards
from the 0, 0.
And this was a total
nightmare because--
I'll tell you why in a sec.
To do that, we actually used
the relational reprojection
platform that were made
by twp Berkeley alum, Will
Payne and Eve McGlynn,
which actually is based,
rather than
Cartesian space, they
based that on Hagerstrandian
conceptions of relational space.
And so, basically,
the idea is that you
can put in certain
forms of data,
and it will reproject
it in a way that
is based in
relationality rather than
a kind of quadratic geometry.
And so we used that.
And then I was like,
OK, but what view
do you want to look from?
Do you want to look from
the side or the top down?
And they're like, does there
only have to be one view?
And I'm like, this multiplicity
is driving me absolutely insane.
And I was like, ah, actually,
that's very difficult
to compute, which is why
I had to hand draw it.
And so, in the end, we've
actually got three views
looking down, looking
across, and then looking up
at the stars.
I haven't yet figured out how
to bring a multiple viewpoint
into a computational frame.
Anyone's interested
in doing that, help?
And so we now have this map--
the stars are, actually,
if you stand at LeSean,
which is in the center,
and look over Mount Diablo, on
the eve of the winter solstice
the year before-- so
I think it's 1578,
the year before Francis
Drake first put the Bay
Area on the map, that is the
star constellation that you'll
see.
We created a program to
get that right as well.
Accuracy was really important
for them as well as us.
We wanted it to be correct.
So this is an example
of this kind of work.
But I also do more
experimental work as well.
So I'm working on my next book,
which is called Cartotopia,
and thinking about
histories of normalization.
For me, I think we
unfairly cast aspersions
at artificial
intelligence and machine
learning because we expect it to
do things that it's not really
designed to do.
And so what I'm doing
is I have data sets
of very large-scale
data sets of maps,
and I'm basically running them
through different generative
adversarial networks to see if I
can get the networks to actually
reproduce these maps.
And they're bad.
I'm not pretending
that these are great,
but they're actually
really, really useful,
using this computation
as a way of understanding
both how AI works, but also the
way in which, historically, maps
have had a role to play in
processes that already exist.
And so this is a map from
the panoramic collection.
And what's really
interesting is that,
actually, in the way in
which the algorithm computes,
you can see a dominance of
certain kinds of landscapes,
specifically
Midwestern landscapes
because of the history
of the data set itself.
And so this is
different cartographers.
And you can see here, Ruger
was an early cartographer
who used this particular
panoramic style.
And he worked mostly
in the Midwest.
And he made far more
maps than anyone
because he was avant garde.
He was an innovator.
And so he basically created the
peak of this kind of mapping.
And then it was perfected
over a period of time.
And you see those
peaks and troughs
in the actual outputs of the
model when it's been trained.
Similarly, here's more
examples of just a lot
of flat Midwestern
landscapes, man.
You also have these
kinds of maps.
This map I was training
on geology maps,
and a colleague of mine
who's a geomorphologist
was like, cool map.
And he looked at closer.
He was like, ew, I
don't like that map.
That's weird.
I'm like, yeah, that's
kind of what AI does.
And he was like, but
can you actually--
could you run a
transect through it?
And I was like,
hold that thought.
Actually, could you do
geomorphological analysis
on a map that has
been generated by AI.
For this, I thought, why not
actually just compute DEM?
So this is Digital
Elevation Model.
So these are 3D
landscape depictions.
And what's particularly
interesting
about these is that, yes, you
can do geomorphology on them,
but I've got a
bunch of interviews
with geomorphologists,
and I've asked them
what kind of landscape is this?
Where is this?
And every single one of
them, for about 20 minutes,
they're looking at it going,
it is definitely a landscape,
but it's nowhere.
I think this kind of comes
with a fundamental question
that we can ask of
machine learning, which
is the point of machine
learning is to normalize.
It's to curve fit.
It's to try and bring out the
most common elements of any kind
of data set and reproduce them.
The issue we have
is geographers,
and I think the fundamental
question around geo AI--
and I'm invited to speak a lot
on a lot of panels around GIS--
is that landscapes themselves
are actually not normalized.
They're actually
deeply uneven because
of seismic and different other
kinds of environmental factors.
So you'll have large
mountain ranges, volcanoes.
You have these spaces
that are abnormal.
They are not smooth and clean.
And what even a badly
trained model does
is it actually tries to
figure out and generalize
a feature that is not
really that general.
And I think this kind
of points, for me,
the question, the argument
I'm making the book
is that, actually, these
processes of normalization
predate machine learning.
Machine learning is
incredibly useful
where you need a process that
does exactly what it does.
It's incredibly useful for
medical imaging, for instance.
We have big data sets.
It's really useful for
doing fairly mundane tasks.
It's useful in a lot
of disability work
as well because we are normal.
Society normalizes.
There are parts
of society, there
are parts of the
environment, there
are parts of the landscape which
are not really fully normal.
And this is where we
need to ask questions.
And I think the final one.
So this is Sanborn.
This is where a lot of
these ideas-- so Sanborn,
I hate this data set.
So I don't know if
many of you actually do
research in machine learning.
But this is the mapping
of the different
whether or it's training.
And you can see the mode
collapse happens again and again
and again.
And I'm really struggling to
get it past a certain step
without falling
into mode collapse.
And I asked a
bunch of colleagues
who are computer
scientists, what do I do?
They're like, you need
to vary your data set.
Well, the problem I have is that
Sanborn was a form of mapping
that happened in
the 19th century.
It's urban mapping, and
it's designed for risk.
So what would happen is they
would go around and survey
the different materials
within a landscape,
map them, color them
according to whether or not--
I think there were four
colors-- how much risk
there was of catastrophic fire.
They would give it to an
insurer who would then decide,
are they overinvested
in a certain area?
So the insurers would use these
maps to decide whether or not
they're going to insure
certain buildings.
The issue is that, firstly, this
was at a time when 19th century
urban planning was
favoring the grid.
It wasn't these big
diagonals of medieval cities.
It was rectilinear grid systems
that you see, particularly
in North America, where a
lot of Sanborn was made.
So the city itself is
already being normalized.
If you went and looked at a map
of Chicago or parts of New York
without labels,
you may not even be
able to tell the
difference between which
is which because the
city itself kind of looks
the same from the top down.
So you already have this
process of normalization.
And then, secondly,
what would happen
is when something would
burn down, fire insurers,
developers would go in,
look at the Sanborn risk,
and then rebuild those areas to
have as low risk as possible,
essentially saying, we're going
to have a fire hydrant every so
feet.
We want the buildings to
look in a particular way.
And so they were regularizing
the landscape as well.
So you get this
iterative process
that is actually not too unlike
what the algorithm itself
is doing.
And so, for me, this
is not necessarily
a failure but a kind of example.
And I've had a conversation
with a bunch of sociologists
about this.
They're like, I don't
know about this AI.
I'm like, guys, you've been
talking about social statistics
since the 19th century.
You know the fundamental
processes here.
And you use social statistics,
actually, in demography,
in computational social science.
It's not such a
terrifying thing.
It's just actually about
understanding, really, what
are these networks good for?
What does a convolution do?
And then, finally-- and this
is like the last project--
this is a project in progress.
This is one that kind
of happened upon me.
And I'm still not sure entirely
where we're going with it.
And so this project is we call
it a geospatial sea of islands.
And it's basically this question
of how do we map the Pacific?
So much of our mapping tradition
and the way in which we think
about mapping is land-based--
point, line, polygon.
There's not really a point,
line, or polygon in the ocean.
It's designed for land
and landform features.
And so we're trying to
think about, actually,
how we remap the Pacific.
And it came to us because
one of my students
was basically interested in--
she had a database
of films that had
been made by Pacific Islanders.
It's like, can you make a map.
And like, sure, easy.
Put some points on a map.
No, it's also been
three years later.
Actually, there's a
fundamental difference
between the way in which
people within the Pacific
imagine that space and the way
in which cartographers and GIS
scientists are not
gastrointestinal scientists.
Geographic
information scientists
actually construct that space.
And so we started
with Emily Hofer,
who in 1994 describes there's a
difference between understanding
the Pacific as a
series of islands
in a vast sea that are all
separate and disparate--
instead, understanding
the Pacific
as a sea of islands in which the
islands all have connections.
And so we're thinking
about how do we
actually try and understand
why don't we map like that?
What are we actually
dealing with?
And then what solutions
are available to us?
And this was sort of beyond
my singular capacity.
So I assembled a team of--
and it's often hard,
as well, to find
researchers who can work with
me because they require domain
specialty as well as knowledge
of computation and code and data
science.
And so we have Sophia, who
came to us with the project.
So she's the Indigenous
tech coordinator
for the Berkeley
Center for New Media
and also cofounder of the
Critical Pacific Islands Studies
Collective.
And then three undergraduates,
Richard Villagomez,
who is in EECS and data
science, who himself
is from Saipan in the Pacific,
and then Elizabeth Fiske,
who is a data
science/geographer.
I think I saw her here-- yes--
and Zac Thorpe, who is also a
